Recital 79 of the GDPR. Requires clear allocation of responsibility, including joint controllers and processor relationships. Background for Articles 26 and 28.

Recital 80 of the GDPR. Explains the EU representative obligation (Article 27): non-EU controllers/processors must designate a representative unless processing is occasional, not large-scale special-category/criminal data, and low-risk, or the entity is a public authority. The representative is subject to enforcement and acts under written mandate.

Recital 81 of the GDPR. Sets controller duties when selecting and contracting processors: sufficient guarantees, written contract or other legal act setting subject matter, duration, nature/purposes, data types, subject categories, and post-processing return/deletion. Recognises Commission/SA standard contractual clauses. Maps to Article 28.
Recital 82 of the GDPR. Records-of-processing recital: controllers and processors must maintain records and cooperate with supervisory authorities by making them available. Read with Article 30.

Recital 83 of the GDPR. Security-of-processing recital: requires risk-evaluated technical and organisational measures (e.g. encryption) appropriate to the state of the art, costs, and risks. Lists examples of harm (accidental/unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure). Anchor for Article 32.

Recital 84 of the GDPR. Justifies the data-protection impact assessment under Article 35: required where processing is likely to result in high risk; outcome must drive mitigation. If residual high risk remains, prior consultation with the supervisory authority is required (Article 36).

Recital 85 of the GDPR. Breach-notification-to-SA recital. Lists harms and sets the 72-hour notification deadline for personal data breaches unless the controller can demonstrate no risk to rights and freedoms. Allows phased information and reasons for delay. Maps to Article 33.

Recital 86 of the GDPR. Breach-communication-to-data-subjects recital: required where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to rights and freedoms; describes content (nature, mitigation recommendations) and emphasises cooperation with the supervisory authority. Maps to Article 34.
Recital 87 of the GDPR. Sets factors for assessing 'without undue delay' breach notification: nature, gravity, and consequences of the breach, including adverse effects on data subjects.

Recital 88 of the GDPR. Calls for detailed format/procedure rules for breach notification that consider whether technical protection (e.g. encryption) was in place, and that respect law-enforcement investigative interests.

Recital 89 of the GDPR. Explains the abolition of general notification of processing under Directive 95/46/EC in favour of a targeted, risk-based regime focused on high-risk processing (new technologies, novel processing, time-elapsed reassessment).

Recital 90 of the GDPR. Companion to Recital 84: details that the DPIA must, before processing, assess high-risk likelihood and severity and document the measures, safeguards, and mechanisms used to mitigate.

Recital 91 of the GDPR. Lists DPIA triggers: large-scale processing at regional/national/supranational level, novel technologies, profiling-based decisions, large-scale special-category or criminal data, large-scale systematic monitoring of public areas, and any operation the supervisory authority considers high-risk. Excludes individual physicians/lawyers from 'large scale'. Frequently cited for DPIA scoping.

Recital 92 of the GDPR. Permits broader DPIA scope where multiple controllers (e.g. a sector or a horizontal platform) plan a common processing environment, allowing a single assessment to cover the shared activity.
Recital 93 of the GDPR. Allows DPIAs to be carried out at the legislative stage when Member State law underpins public-authority processing, mirroring Article 35(10).

Recital 94 of the GDPR. Prior-consultation recital (Article 36): mandatory where residual high risk cannot be mitigated. Supervisory authority must respond within a specified period; silence does not waive its powers (including prohibition). DPIA outputs and mitigation measures should be submitted.
Recital 95 of the GDPR. Requires the processor to assist the controller, on request, with DPIA and prior-consultation obligations. Read with Article 28(3)(f).

Recital 96 of the GDPR. Suggests consulting the supervisory authority during the preparation of legislative/regulatory measures providing for processing, to ensure GDPR compliance and to mitigate risk. Background for Article 36(4).

Recital 97 of the GDPR. Explains when a DPO is required (Article 37): public authorities, controllers whose core activities involve regular and systematic large-scale monitoring, or large-scale processing of special-category or criminal data. Defines 'core activities' as primary, not ancillary, and stresses DPO independence.
Recital 98 of the GDPR. Encourages associations and bodies representing controllers/processors to draft codes of conduct calibrated to sectoral risk and SME specifics. Read with Article 40.
Recital 99 of the GDPR. Requires association/body consultation with stakeholders, including data subjects where feasible, when drafting or amending a code of conduct.
Recital 100 of the GDPR. Encourages certification mechanisms, data-protection seals, and marks so data subjects can rapidly assess product/service compliance. Background for Articles 42 and 43.

Recital 101 of the GDPR. Sets the policy frame for Chapter V international transfers: third-country flows are necessary for trade but must not undermine GDPR protection, including in onward transfers. Read with Articles 44 et seq.

Recital 102 of the GDPR. Preserves international agreements between the Union and third countries that regulate transfers with appropriate safeguards. Allows Member State agreements within strict limits.

Recital 103 of the GDPR. Frames the Article 45 adequacy decision: the Commission may declare a third country, territory, sector, or international organisation adequate, eliminating the need for further authorisation. Decisions may be revoked after notice. Background for adequacy proceedings.

Recital 104 of the GDPR. Lists the criteria the Commission must weigh in adequacy assessments: rule of law, access to justice, human-rights norms, sectoral and general law (including national-security and criminal law), independent supervision, cooperation mechanisms, and effective redress. Foundational for the Schrems I/II line.

Recital 105 of the GDPR. Requires the Commission to consider a third country's participation in multilateral systems, accession to the Council of Europe Convention 108 and its Additional Protocol, and to consult the EDPB during adequacy assessments.

Recital 106 of the GDPR. Adequacy-decision monitoring recital: the Commission must periodically review decisions, consult third countries, and report findings to the comitology committee, Parliament, and Council.

Recital 107 of the GDPR. Mechanism for revoking adequacy: where a third country no longer ensures adequacy, transfers are prohibited unless safeguards or derogations apply; the Commission consults the third country in good faith.

Recital 108 of the GDPR. Sets the role of appropriate safeguards under Article 46 in the absence of adequacy: BCRs, standard contractual clauses (Commission or SA-adopted), ad hoc contractual clauses, and administrative arrangements between public bodies. Safeguards must deliver enforceable rights and effective remedies; non-binding arrangements need supervisory authority authorisation.

Recital 109 of the GDPR. Confirms that controllers/processors may embed standard contractual clauses in broader contracts and add supplementary safeguards, provided they do not contradict the SCCs or undermine data-subject rights. Backbone of Schrems II 'supplementary measures' reasoning.

Recital 110 of the GDPR. Binding-corporate-rules recital: a group of undertakings (or joint economic activity) may use approved BCRs for intra-group international transfers, provided BCRs include essential principles and enforceable rights. Read with Article 47.

Recital 111 of the GDPR. Frames Article 49 derogations for transfers without adequacy or appropriate safeguards: explicit consent, occasional contract or legal-claim necessity, important public-interest grounds, and registers established by law. Sets limits on register-based transfers.

Recital 112 of the GDPR. Elaborates examples of important public-interest derogations (Article 49(1)(d)): inter-authority exchanges (competition, tax, customs, financial supervision, social security, public health, anti-doping). Includes humanitarian transfers under Geneva Conventions.

Recital 113 of the GDPR. Compelling-legitimate-interests derogation (Article 49(1) subparagraph 2): permits non-repetitive transfers concerning a limited number of data subjects where overriding interests, assessment of all circumstances, and suitable safeguards exist. Controller must inform the supervisory authority and the data subject.

Recital 114 of the GDPR. Where no adequacy decision exists, controllers/processors must use solutions that preserve enforceable, effective data-subject rights post-transfer. Residual safety-net framing for Chapter V.

Recital 115 of the GDPR. Addresses third-country laws that purport to require disclosure of personal data extraterritorially without an international agreement. Transfers must still comply with Chapter V; disclosure may sometimes be necessary for important public-interest grounds in Union or Member State law. Foundational for Article 48 analysis.

Recital 116 of the GDPR. Recognises challenges of cross-border enforcement (jurisdictional reach, resource constraints, inconsistent regimes) and supports international cooperation between supervisory authorities and the Commission with third-country counterparts on a reciprocity basis.

Recital 117 of the GDPR. Establishes the independence of supervisory authorities as essential, and allows Member States to set up more than one supervisory authority to reflect constitutional/administrative structure. Read with Article 51.
Recital 118 of the GDPR. Clarifies that supervisory authority independence does not preclude control or monitoring of financial expenditure or judicial review.
Recital 119 of the GDPR. Where a Member State has multiple supervisory authorities, it must designate a single contact point for the consistency mechanism and ensure their effective participation.
Recital 120 of the GDPR. Requires that each supervisory authority be adequately resourced (financial, human, infrastructure) and have a separate public budget. Backstop for Article 52(4).

Recital 121 of the GDPR. Governs appointment, integrity, and independence of supervisory authority members: transparent appointment by parliament, government, or independent body, prohibition on incompatible occupations, and own-staff control. Read with Articles 53-54.

Recital 122 of the GDPR. Defines the territorial competence of each supervisory authority: establishments on its territory, public-interest processing, processing affecting subjects on its territory, and non-EU-controller targeting of its residents. Covers complaints, investigations, and awareness.

Recital 123 of the GDPR. Tasks supervisory authorities with consistent application and cooperation with each other and the Commission without needing inter-state agreements. Background for Chapter VII.

Recital 124 of the GDPR. Sets the lead-supervisory-authority rule for cross-border processing under Article 56: the SA of the main or single establishment leads, while other concerned SAs participate. Complainant SAs are also concerned SAs. EDPB may guide on 'substantial effect' and 'relevant and reasoned objection'.

Recital 125 of the GDPR. Confirms the lead SA's power to adopt binding decisions while requiring close coordination with concerned SAs; complaint-rejection decisions remain with the SA that received the complaint.

Recital 126 of the GDPR. Joint decisions of lead and concerned SAs are directed to and binding on the controller/processor at its main or single establishment, which must implement the measures across its EU processing.

Recital 127 of the GDPR. Sets the 'local case' track: an SA may handle matters confined to a single Member State even where the controller is multi-state, subject to informing the lead SA, which decides whether the one-stop-shop applies. Reflects flexibility within Article 56.

Recital 128 of the GDPR. Disapplies the one-stop-shop for public authorities or private bodies processing in the public interest; only the SA of the Member State where the body is established is competent.

Recital 129 of the GDPR. Sets requirements for supervisory powers (investigation, correction, sanctions, authorisation, advice), procedural safeguards (impartiality, hearing rights, judicial authorisation for premises), and formal requirements for binding measures (writing, reasoning, signature). Workhorse recital for Article 58 analysis.

Recital 130 of the GDPR. Where the complaint-receiving SA is not the lead, the lead must coordinate closely and take utmost account of the receiving SA's view, while the receiving SA remains competent for territorial investigation.

Recital 131 of the GDPR. Sets the amicable-settlement track for local-only infringements; if unsuccessful, the receiving SA exercises its full powers. Lists processing categories (territory-specific operations, targeted offers, MS-law-driven assessments).
Recital 132 of the GDPR. Mandates awareness-raising by supervisory authorities targeted at controllers/processors (including SMEs), natural persons, and educational contexts. Pointer recital.
Recital 133 of the GDPR. Mutual-assistance recital: SAs must assist each other; an SA receiving no response within one month may adopt a provisional measure. Read with Article 61.
Recital 134 of the GDPR. Encourages joint operations between SAs and requires the requested SA to respond within a specified time period.

Recital 135 of the GDPR. Establishes the consistency mechanism (Article 63) to ensure uniform application across the Union, particularly where measures substantially affect data subjects in multiple Member States.

Recital 136 of the GDPR. Empowers the EDPB to issue opinions and binding decisions in disputes between SAs (two-thirds majority for legally binding decisions in clearly specified cases of conflict). Background for Article 65.

Recital 137 of the GDPR. Permits a supervisory authority to adopt urgent, duly justified provisional measures of up to three months where data-subject rights need immediate protection. Read with Article 66.

Recital 138 of the GDPR. Makes the consistency mechanism a precondition for lawfulness of measures where its application is mandatory; in other cross-border cases, the cooperation mechanism, mutual assistance, and joint operations may proceed bilaterally without triggering the consistency procedure.

Recital 139 of the GDPR. Sets out the EDPB as an independent Union body with legal personality, replacing the Article 29 Working Party, composed of national SA heads and the EDPS, with the Commission participating without voting rights. Read with Article 68.
Recital 140 of the GDPR. Sets the EDPB secretariat at the EDPS, with EDPB-dedicated staff acting exclusively on EDPB Chair instructions. Background for Article 75.

Recital 141 of the GDPR. Right to lodge a complaint with the supervisory authority of habitual residence and to an effective judicial remedy under Article 47 Charter; SAs must inform complainants of progress within a reasonable period. Read with Articles 77-78.

Recital 142 of the GDPR. Permits data subjects to mandate a not-for-profit body, active in data protection, to lodge complaints and exercise judicial remedies on their behalf, and (where Member State law allows) compensation claims. Member States may also empower such bodies to act without mandate. Article 80 framing.

Recital 143 of the GDPR. Details judicial-review pathways: actions for annulment of EDPB decisions before the CJEU under Article 263 TFEU within two months, national-court remedies against binding SA decisions, preliminary references under Article 267 TFEU, and the rule that national courts cannot invalidate EDPB decisions unilaterally. Heavyweight recital for procedural questions.

Recital 144 of the GDPR. Coordination of related proceedings across Member States: a later-seized court should contact the earlier-seized court to confirm related proceedings and may stay or decline jurisdiction. Read with Article 81.

Recital 145 of the GDPR. Plaintiff choice of forum under Article 79(2): claims against controllers/processors may be brought where the establishment is located or where the data subject resides, except against public authorities exercising public powers.

Recital 146 of the GDPR. Establishes the right to compensation under Article 82: broad construction of 'damage' along CJEU case-law, joint and several liability where multiple actors are involved in the same processing, and a controller/processor's exemption only if not in any way responsible. Allows recourse between liable actors after full compensation.
Recital 147 of the GDPR. Confirms that GDPR-specific jurisdiction rules prevail over general jurisdiction rules in Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 (Brussels I recast).

Recital 148 of the GDPR. Frames administrative-fine policy: penalties must reinforce enforcement; reprimands may replace fines for minor infringements or disproportionate burdens on natural persons. Lists the aggravating/mitigating factors (nature, gravity, duration, intent, mitigation, responsibility, previous infringements, cooperation, code adherence). Read with Article 83.

Recital 149 of the GDPR. Allows Member States to lay down criminal penalties (and profit-deprivation measures) for infringements, subject to the ne bis in idem principle as interpreted by the CJEU. Read with Article 84.

Recital 150 of the GDPR. Administrative-fine recital: SAs must set fines individually, considering all circumstances; 'undertaking' takes its TFEU competition-law meaning; the consistency mechanism may harmonise fines. Member States choose whether and how public authorities are fined.

Recital 151 of the GDPR. Denmark/Estonia carve-out: their legal systems do not allow administrative fines as conceived in the Regulation, so equivalent fines may be imposed by criminal courts (Denmark) or in misdemeanour procedures (Estonia), provided they are effective, proportionate, and dissuasive.
Recital 152 of the GDPR. Where the GDPR does not harmonise penalties, Member States must provide effective, proportionate, and dissuasive penalties of their choosing (criminal or administrative).

Recital 153 of the GDPR. Mandates Member State derogations to reconcile the right to data protection with freedom of expression and information (journalism, academic, artistic, literary expression) per Charter Article 11. Calls for a broad interpretation of journalism and lists the substantive areas where derogations may apply. Read with Article 85.

Recital 154 of the GDPR. Allows Member State law to reconcile public access to official documents and reuse of public-sector information (Directive 2003/98/EC) with data protection. Read with Article 86.

Recital 155 of the GDPR. Permits Member State law or collective agreements (including 'works agreements') to provide specific rules on employee personal data processing (recruitment, contract performance, work organisation, equality, H&S, employment-rights exercise, termination). Read with Article 88.

Recital 156 of the GDPR. Sets safeguards for processing for archiving/research/statistics purposes: technical and organisational measures (including pseudonymisation), assessment of feasibility of de-identification, and Member State authority to derogate from rights (information, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection). Read with Article 89.

Recital 157 of the GDPR. Underlines the societal value of registry-based research (cardiovascular disease, cancer, depression; social sciences) and supports processing for scientific research subject to safeguards in Union or Member State law.

Recital 158 of the GDPR. Archiving recital: GDPR applies to archiving processing (but not to deceased persons); defines public-interest archive holders and allows Member States to authorise archiving related to totalitarian regimes, genocide, crimes against humanity (including the Holocaust), and war crimes.

Recital 159 of the GDPR. Broad construction of scientific research: includes technological development, demonstration, fundamental and applied research, privately funded research, and public-health studies. References Article 179(1) TFEU European Research Area objective. Background for Article 89(2) derogations.
Recital 160 of the GDPR. Historical-research recital: includes historical research and genealogy, while reiterating GDPR does not apply to deceased persons.
Recital 161 of the GDPR. Cross-references Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 (Clinical Trials Regulation) for consent in clinical-trial participation.

Recital 162 of the GDPR. Statistical-purposes recital: requires Member State or Union law to define statistical content, access, and safeguards. Defines statistical purposes as producing aggregate, non-decisional results; statistical outputs cannot support measures or decisions about specific natural persons.
Recital 163 of the GDPR. Protects the confidentiality of European and national statistics, citing Article 338(2) TFEU principles and Regulation (EC) No 223/2009 on European statistics.

Recital 164 of the GDPR. Allows Member State law to safeguard professional secrecy obligations vis-à-vis supervisory authority access to data and premises, without prejudice to existing Union-law secrecy rules. Read with Article 90.
Recital 165 of the GDPR. Preserves the constitutional status of churches and religious associations under Article 17 TFEU. Read with Article 91.

Recital 166 of the GDPR. Delegates power to the Commission under Article 290 TFEU to adopt delegated acts on certification criteria/requirements and on standardised icon information and procedures. Read with Article 92.
Recital 167 of the GDPR. Confers implementing powers on the Commission under Regulation (EU) No 182/2011, with attention to SME-specific measures. Read with Article 93.

Recital 168 of the GDPR. Lists the implementing acts to be adopted via examination procedure: SCCs between controllers/processors and between processors, codes of conduct, certification technical standards, adequacy specifics, standard protection clauses, BCR formats, mutual-assistance arrangements, and inter-authority data-exchange formats.
Recital 169 of the GDPR. Permits immediately applicable implementing acts where evidence shows a third country no longer ensures adequacy and urgency so requires.

Recital 170 of the GDPR. Subsidiarity and proportionality recital: the objectives (equivalent protection and free flow) can be better achieved at Union level; the Regulation does not go beyond what is necessary. Standard treaty-basis recital.

Recital 171 of the GDPR. Transitional recital: repeals Directive 95/46/EC; ongoing processing must be brought into conformity within two years; pre-GDPR consents remain valid if consistent with GDPR conditions; Commission decisions and SA authorisations under 95/46/EC remain in force until amended/replaced/repealed.
Recital 172 of the GDPR. Records consultation with the European Data Protection Supervisor under Article 28(2) of Regulation 45/2001 and the EDPS opinion of 7 March 2012. Procedural-history recital.

Recital 173 of the GDPR. Sets the relationship with the ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC: GDPR applies to matters not subject to specific obligations under that Directive, which should be amended/reviewed to ensure consistency. Important for interpreting GDPR/ePrivacy boundaries (cookies, e-marketing).
